summary: Triclosan is a synthetic broad-spectrum antibacterial and antifungal agent formerly common in soaps, hand washes, toothpastes and consumer antiseptics. It acts mainly by inhibiting bacterial fatty-acid synthesis (the enoyl-ACP reductase enzyme FabI). Its use is now heavily RESTRICTED: the US FDA banned it from over-the-counter consumer antiseptic wash products (2016) and from consumer antiseptic rubs (2017) for lack of demonstrated benefit over plain soap and unresolved safety questions, and the EU has restricted it. Concerns include antimicrobial resistance, endocrine-disruption signals in animal studies, and skin sensitisation. It is not an FDA-approved therapeutic drug; this record is compiled from regulatory and monograph sources.
indications: Topical antiseptic/antibacterial in certain permitted products (e.g. some toothpaste for gingivitis where still approved, surgical or healthcare-specific products per local regulation)
Preservative/antimicrobial additive in some cosmetics within regulatory concentration limits
Note: banned/withdrawn from US OTC consumer antibacterial soaps and hand sanitisers

dosage.d: Used at low concentrations within regulatory limits (commonly up to ~0.3% in cosmetics; ~0.3% in some toothpastes)
dosage.n: Concentration set by the product, not patient-titrated

dosage.d: Apply the finished product to the skin as directed and rinse; do not ingest
dosage.n: Subject to local regulatory approval; many consumer uses now prohibited

admin: For external/topical use only - do not swallow oral-care products beyond normal use
Apply the finished product as directed on the label and rinse off skin cleansers thoroughly
Avoid contact with the eyes; rinse if contact occurs
Discontinue if skin irritation, rash or sensitisation develops
Keep out of reach of children
moa: At the concentrations used in consumer products triclosan is largely bacteriostatic, acting by binding and inhibiting bacterial enoyl-acyl carrier protein reductase (FabI), a key enzyme in fatty-acid biosynthesis, thereby disrupting bacterial cell-membrane synthesis. At higher concentrations it has broader, more bactericidal membrane-disrupting effects.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to triclosan or product components
relative: Use over large areas or prolonged/repeated exposure (endocrine and resistance concerns)
Use in infants and during pregnancy/lactation (minimise exposure)
monitor: Local skin tolerance and signs of sensitisation/contact dermatitis

preg: Avoid deliberate or prolonged use and minimise exposure during pregnancy. Triclosan crosses the placenta and animal studies have raised endocrine (thyroid/oestrogen) signals; human safety in pregnancy is not established.
lact: Triclosan has been detected in human breast milk in proportion to maternal exposure. Although clinical harm to infants has not been demonstrated, exposure should be minimised during breastfeeding.
renal: Not relevant for topical use; systemic clearance is not the basis for any dose adjustment in normal external use.
hepatic: Not relevant for topical use. Absorbed triclosan is conjugated (glucuronidated/sulfated) and excreted, but topical exposure does not warrant hepatic dose adjustment.

moderate: Other topical antiseptics (no clear benefit to combining; potential additive irritation)
minor: Cationic surfactants and some formulation excipients may reduce activity
interactions.diagnostics: No significant interference with laboratory tests at normal topical exposure

serious: Possible contribution to antimicrobial cross-resistance (population-level concern)

monitoring: No routine systemic monitoring needed for normal topical use
counsel: This is for external use only - do not swallow
Plain soap and water is as effective as antibacterial soap for everyday hand hygiene
Stop using and seek advice if you develop a rash, redness or itching
Avoid getting it in the eyes
Many consumer antibacterial products containing triclosan have been withdrawn - check labels
pk: Antibacterial effect on contact during use
Acts locally at the site of application
Absorbed fraction has an elimination half-life of roughly 11-21 hours (conjugated and excreted)
Some residual substantivity on skin/oral surfaces; effect is short-lived
Store the finished product at room temperature as per its label, away from children
pearls: Not an FDA-approved therapeutic drug; the FDA removed triclosan from OTC consumer antibacterial wash soaps (2016) and consumer antiseptic rubs (2017) - no proven benefit over plain soap and unresolved safety data (this record is based on regulatory/monograph sources)
Primary mechanism is inhibition of bacterial FabI (enoyl-ACP reductase) in fatty-acid synthesis
Concerns driving restriction: potential antimicrobial resistance, animal endocrine-disruption signals, and skin sensitisation
Detectable in human urine and breast milk, reflecting widespread historical exposure
Still permitted in some specific products (e.g. certain toothpastes for gingivitis, defined healthcare products) within strict concentration limits depending on jurisdiction
missed: Not applicable - triclosan is used within antiseptic/cosmetic products on an as-needed basis, not on a prescribed dosing schedule.
overdose: Significant toxicity from normal topical use is not expected. Accidental ingestion of triclosan-containing products may cause gastrointestinal upset; large ingestions could theoretically cause CNS depression. Manage supportively, do not induce vomiting routinely, and seek poison-centre advice for substantial ingestion.
